$comment: Why this case is in the corpus: it is the only one where the number of findings attributed to a
registry row is strictly between zero and the number of violations the verdict declares. Every other
case attributes all of them or none of them, so loosening findingsFromReport's guard from
`findings.length < declared` to `findings.length === 0 && declared > 0` reproduces the whole corpus
without it. A real run that attributed seven of eight would then be scored as 7 of 9 recall instead
of refused, which is the exact confusion the guard exists to prevent.
The report is CONSTRUCTED, from misses-two's report with one more Medium counted. The CLI parser
permits that: assertFindingCountsAgree binds Critical and High exactly in both directions and bounds
Medium and Low in one direction only, because summarizing a counted Medium in prose is the shape live
derivation: The verdict declares 4 Critical, 3 High, 1 Medium and 0 Low, which sums to 8.
The report carries seven finding blocks, each with a Location line followed by a Row line: C1, C3, C4,
C5, H1, H3 and H4. The eighth violation is the Medium, which the report counts in its Total Violations
line and describes in the naming-notes prose without a Location or a Row. Seven findings are
7 is fewer than 8, so findingsFromReport returns null and scoreVerdict returns null with it. The seven
attributed rows are never matched against the plants, so recall is not 7 of 9; it does not exist.
That is the whole point of the case. Those seven rows are real hits against real plants, and a scorer
that scored them anyway would publish 0.7778 recall for a run whose report contract had moved. The
shortfall is one violation, the smallest a report can have, and the rule is a comparison rather than a
The verdict's own numbers come from cli/lib/parse-report.js reading this report:
100 - 4x10 - 3x5 - 1x2 - 0x1 = 43, and any Critical at all forces Block.
